place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆 · 十一月

setup.zh: 院系杯小组赛，他抢到头一个篮板，落地崴了右脚。「疼和伤，是两本账。」阿禾单脚闭眼站给他看：崴过脚的，都得练这个。
setup.en: The group stage of the cup: his first rebound, and he lands on his right ankle. "Pain and injury are two different accounts." Ahe stands on one foot, eyes shut, to show him: everyone who sprains an ankle has to do this.

recap.zh: 崴了右踝；「疼和伤，是两本账」；单脚闭眼，三秒。
recap.en: A sprained right ankle; "pain and injury are two accounts"; one foot, eyes shut, three seconds.

en: One foot, eyes shut: three seconds.

story.zh:
十一月二十五日夜里十一点，沈芒看着马桶里一泡可乐色的尿，头一个念头不是「我要死了」，是：不许让阿禾知道。

这句话，四天前他就对自己说过一回。

十一月十四日，小组赛第二轮，阿禾给了他五分钟。他抢到了院系杯的头一个篮板，落地时右脚踩在别人脚面上，脚踝往外一翻，「咯」的一声，他自己都听见了。

校医捏了捏，说外踝韧带拉伤，开了护踝和一对拐。沈芒问：「几天能好？」校医说：「一两个礼拜左右就不疼了。但完全恢复，至少需要三个月。」

他只听进去了前半句：第三轮在一个礼拜以后，不疼就能上。

礼拜二下了针灸实验课，他蹭到讲台边，撩起裤腿，露出肿得像发面馒头的脚踝：「严老师，给我这儿扎两针，礼拜六能上场吗？」

严老师看了一会儿，回身在黑板上写了一行：「所言节者，神气之所游行出入也，非皮肉筋骨也。」「《灵枢》头一篇。扎针，能让你少疼一点，不能让你这根筋长得快一点。疼和伤，是两本账。你那根筋，得它自己长。」

那天晚上，阿禾上六楼送绷带。她把绷带往桌上一放，抬起一只脚，闭上眼，单脚站着，纹丝不动：「崴过脚的，都得练这个。韧带长得慢，比肉慢多了。而且一崴，管脚的那些神经也伤了，脑子不知道脚踩在哪儿，所以老崴。每天闭着眼单脚站，站到一分钟不晃。」

他扶着桌沿试了一回。一闭眼，整个人像插在烂泥里的竹竿，两只胳膊乱划，第三秒上，好脚「啪」地踩实了地。

「三秒。」阿禾说。
story.en:
At eleven o'clock on the night of November 25th, Shen Mang stood looking at a stream of cola-coloured urine in the toilet. His first thought was not "I'm dying." It was: Ahe must not find out.

He had said that same sentence to himself four days earlier.

November 14th, second round of the group stage. Ahe gave him five minutes. He grabbed his first rebound of the inter-college cup, and when he came down his right foot landed on someone else's; the ankle rolled outward with a "crack" that even he could hear.

The school doctor felt it, said a sprained lateral ankle ligament, and gave him a brace and a pair of crutches. Shen Mang asked, "How many days till it's better?" The doctor said, "The pain should be gone in a week or two. But a full recovery takes at least three months."

He only heard the first half: round three was a week away, and once it stopped hurting he could play.

On Tuesday, after acupuncture lab, he edged up to the lectern, rolled up his trouser leg and showed an ankle swollen like a steamed bun: "Teacher Yan, if you put a couple of needles in here, can I play on Saturday?"

Teacher Yan looked at it for a moment, then turned and wrote a line on the blackboard: "What are called the joints are where the spirit-qi travels, goes out and comes in; they are not skin, flesh, sinew or bone." "The first chapter of the Lingshu. Needles can make it hurt a little less. They can't make that ligament of yours grow back any faster. Pain and injury are two different accounts. That ligament has to grow back on its own."

That night Ahe came up to the sixth floor with bandages. She set them on the desk, lifted one foot, shut her eyes and stood on one leg without a wobble: "Everyone who sprains an ankle has to do this. Ligaments heal slowly, far slower than muscle. And a sprain damages the nerves in the foot too — your brain stops knowing where your foot is, so you keep rolling it. Stand on one foot with your eyes shut every day, until you can do a minute without wobbling."

He tried it once, holding the edge of the desk. The moment he shut his eyes he was a bamboo pole stuck in mud, both arms flailing; on the third second his good foot slapped down on the floor.

"Three seconds," said Ahe.
